CHAPTER W · ELECTIVE AREA · JUNE

Counting and calculating – then and now

Our digits 0 to 9 are not all that old. The Egyptians painted strokes, hobbles and lotus flowers, the Romans wrote letters, the Maya dots and bars. In Saxony, Adam Ries taught people to calculate with counters on lines and with the pen. And today every computer calculates with only two digits. In this chapter you travel through the history of numbers.

8 LESSONS3 UNITS3 LABS
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • read and write numbers in the script of the Egyptians and the Romans
  • understand the base-20 system of the Maya with its zero
  • how Adam Ries calculated on the lines and why he is so famous in Saxony
  • count, add and subtract in the binary system and in the base-5 system

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Numbers of the Egyptians and the Romans

MDCCCLXXII means $1000 + 500 + 300 + 50 + 20 + 2 = 1872$. If you want to calculate with it, you first have to take everything apart. That is why the Romans calculated with pebbles on a counting board, the abacus, and only wrote down the result.

The scripts of the Egyptians and the Romans are additive systems: every symbol has a fixed value, wherever it stands, and you add all the values. With us, on the other hand, the value of a digit depends on its place. That is called a place value system.

KEY POINT · ROMAN NUMERALS

I = 1 · V = 5 · X = 10 · L = 50 · C = 100 · D = 500 · M = 1000

The symbols are written from large to small and added. If a smaller symbol stands in front of a larger one, it is subtracted: IV = 4, IX = 9, XL = 40, XC = 90, CD = 400, CM = 900.

A symbol stands at most three times in a row: 3 = III, but 4 = IV.

Egyptian numerals: a stroke for 1, a hobble (an arch) for 10, a coil of rope for 100, a lotus flower for 1000. For 10,000 they painted a finger, for 100,000 a tadpole.

No zero: neither the Egyptians nor the Romans had a symbol for zero. They did not need one either, because there were no empty places.

INTERACTIVE · ONE NUMBER, FOUR SCRIPTS
EXAMPLE 1 · READING ROMAN NUMERALS

Read a) XLVII   b) MCMXCIX   c) CDXLIV

a) $40 + 7 = 47$   b) $1000 + 900 + 90 + 9 = 1999$   c) $400 + 40 + 4 = 444$

EXAMPLE 2 · WRITING ROMAN NUMERALS

Write 2026 and 349 in Roman numerals.

$2026 = 2000 + 20 + 6$: MMXXVI. $349 = 300 + 40 + 9$: CCCXLIX.

a) 24   b) 88   c) 190   d) 1666

Write in Roman numerals: a) 14   b) 99   c) 444   d) the year you were born

a) XIV   b) XCIX   c) CDXLIV   d) for example 2015 = MMXV

Draw the number 3,254 in Egyptian numerals. How many symbols do you need? How many digits do we need?

3 lotus flowers, 2 coils of rope, 5 hobbles, 4 strokes: 14 symbols. We need 4 digits.

Which number between 1 and 3999 needs the most symbols in Roman numerals?

3888 = MMMDCCCLXXXVIII with 15 symbols.

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2The Maya counted in twenties

The Maya lived in Central America. More than a thousand years ago they already had a place value system, with twenties instead of tens. Their digits for 0 to 19 are made of only three symbols: a dot for 1, a bar for 5 and a shell for zero.

KEY POINT · THE BASE-20 SYSTEM

The levels are written one above the other, the ones at the very bottom. Each level is worth twenty times as much as the one below: 1, 20, 400, 8,000.

Example: at the top 5 (a bar), in the middle 1 (a dot), at the bottom 6 (a bar and a dot): $5 \cdot 400 + 1 \cdot 20 + 6 = 2026$.

The shell shows an empty level: a dot at the top with a shell below means $1 \cdot 20 + 0 = 20$.

Why twenty? Perhaps the Maya counted fingers and toes. French still has a trace of it: 80 is quatre-vingts, “four twenties”.

In Dresden there is one of only four surviving Maya manuscripts, the Codex Dresdensis, full of numbers and calendars. It is on display in the Saxon State Library.

INTERACTIVE · MAYA NUMBERS
EXAMPLE 3 · READING MAYA NUMBERS

At the top there are two dots, below them three bars and a dot. Which number is that?

At the top 2, at the bottom $3 \cdot 5 + 1 = 16$: $2 \cdot 20 + 16$.

56

EXAMPLE 4 · WRITING MAYA NUMBERS

Write 425 in Maya numbers.

$425 = 1 \cdot 400 + 1 \cdot 20 + 5$. A dot at the top, a dot in the middle, a bar at the bottom.

EXERCISES

Draw as a Maya number: a) 7   b) 19   c) 20   d) 45   e) 400

a) a bar with 2 dots above it   b) 3 bars with 4 dots above them   c) 1 dot at the top, a shell at the bottom   d) 2 dots at the top, a bar at the bottom   e) 1 dot at the top, two shells below it

Which number has two bars at the top, a shell in the middle and two dots at the bottom?

$10 \cdot 400 + 0 \cdot 20 + 2 = 4{,}002$

What is the largest number the Maya could write with two levels? What is the largest with three levels?

Two levels: $19 \cdot 20 + 19 = 399$. Three levels: $19 \cdot 400 + 19 \cdot 20 + 19 = 7{,}999$.

TEST YOURSELF!

2 at the top, 16 at the bottom. Which number?

$2 \cdot 20 + 16$

What is a dot worth on the third level from the bottom?

$20 \cdot 20$

UNIT 33 LESSONS

3Adam Ries and the binary system

Adam Ries was born in 1492 in Staffelstein in Franconia and lived from about 1523 in Annaberg in the Ore Mountains, where he died in 1559. He wrote arithmetic books in German, not in Latin like the scholars. That way craftsmen and merchants could learn to calculate. His best-known book appeared in Erfurt in 1522: Rechenung auff der linihen und federn (calculating on the lines and with the pen). In it he explains two ways: calculating with counters on lines and written calculation with the pen and the digits we use today.

KEY POINT · CALCULATING ON THE LINES

On the line board the lines stand for 1, 10, 100, 1000, the spaces in between for 5, 50, 500. To add, you put down the counters of both numbers.

Then you bundle: 5 counters on a line become one in the space above, 2 counters in a space become one on the next line. That is the same as carrying in written addition.

“Nach Adam Ries(e)” (“according to Adam Ries”) is still what people in Germany say when a calculation is sure to be right. At the Adam Ries Museum in Annaberg-Buchholz you can try out calculating on the lines.

INTERACTIVE · THE LINE BOARD

We have ten digits because we have ten fingers. Computers only know two states: current on or off. That is why they calculate in the binary system with the digits 0 and 1. Each place is worth twice as much as the place to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, …

KEY POINT · OTHER PLACE VALUE SYSTEMS

Binary system: $1011_2 = 1 \cdot 8 + 0 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 2 + 1 \cdot 1 = 11$. You count 0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101, 110, 111, 1000, …

Base-5 system: digits 0 to 4, place values 1, 5, 25, 125. $243_5 = 2 \cdot 25 + 4 \cdot 5 + 3 = 73$.

Adding works as usual, only there is a carry as soon as the base is reached: in the binary system $1 + 1 = 10_2$.

INTERACTIVE · IN THE BINARY SYSTEM
EXAMPLE 5 · ADDING IN BINARY

Calculate $101_2 + 11_2$ in the binary system and check in the decimal system.

Ones: $1 + 1 = 10_2$, write 0, carry 1. Twos: $0 + 1 + 1 = 10_2$, write 0, carry 1. Fours: $1 + 1 = 10_2$. Result $1000_2$.

$101_2 + 11_2 = 1000_2$, so $5 + 3 = 8$

EXAMPLE 6 · CONVERTING

Write 25 in the binary system.

The largest power of two up to 25 is 16: $25 = 16 + 8 + 1$. Places 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: 1, 1, 0, 0, 1.

$11001_2$

EXERCISES

Lay out $1492 + 1522$ on the line board and bundle step by step. Write down which bundlings are needed.

Result 3,014. Five counters on the 10 line are bundled into one in the 50 space, two in the 50 space into one on the 100 line, five on the 100 line into one in the 500 space and two in the 500 space into one on the 1000 line.

Write in the decimal system: a) $110_2$   b) $1111_2$   c) $100000_2$   d) $34_5$

a) 6   b) 15   c) 32   d) 19

Write in the binary system: a) 9   b) 20   c) 31   d) 64

a) $1001_2$   b) $10100_2$   c) $11111_2$   d) $1000000_2$

Calculate in the binary system and check: a) $110_2 + 11_2$   b) $1010_2 - 11_2$

a) $1001_2$ ($6 + 3 = 9$)   b) $111_2$ ($10 - 3 = 7$)

With ten fingers you can count much further than 10 in the binary system: each finger is a place, stretched out means 1. Up to which number can you get?

Ten places: $1111111111_2 = 1023$. You can get up to 1,023.

TEST YOURSELF!

Which number is $1011_2$?

$8 + 2 + 1$

Which number is $243_5$?

$50 + 20 + 3$

What does the line board show after $748 + 386$ and all the bundling?

$748 + 386 = 1134$

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Write the number 100 in four ways: in Roman numerals, in Egyptian numerals (describe the symbols), as a Maya number and in the binary system.

C · a coil of rope · 5 at the top (a bar), a shell at the bottom · $1100100_2$

Connecting with chapter 1.2: write the place values as powers: in the decimal system $10^0, 10^1, 10^2$, in the binary system, in the base-5 system, with the Maya.

Binary system $2^0, 2^1, 2^2, 2^3$ = 1, 2, 4, 8 · base-5 system $5^0, 5^1, 5^2$ = 1, 5, 25 · Maya $20^0, 20^1, 20^2$ = 1, 20, 400

In the binary system you can see at once whether a number is even. How? And how can you tell in the base-5 system whether a number is divisible by 5?

Even numbers end in 0 in the binary system. In the base-5 system the multiples of 5 end in 0, just like the multiples of 10 with us.

EXCURSIONHISTORY IN SAXONY

The Maya codex in Dresden

In the treasury of the Saxon State Library in Dresden lies one of the most valuable books in the world: the Codex Dresdensis. It is one of only four Maya manuscripts that survived the conquest of Central America. The book is folded like a concertina, made of bark paper, and several metres long. In 1739 it was bought for the electoral library in Dresden.

Many pages show numbers made of dots, bars and shells. With them the Maya calculated calendars, eclipses of the moon and the sun and the course of Venus. Around 1880 the librarian Ernst Förstemann in Dresden was one of the first to decipher the numbers and tables.

You can look at the codex in the library, and every page can be found online as a digital copy. Look for a shell there!

Sources: SLUB Dresden, Mscr.Dresd.R.310 (Codex Dresdensis), digital copy and exhibition. E. Förstemann: Die Maya-Handschrift der Königlichen öffentlichen Bibliothek zu Dresden. Leipzig 1880.
